segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The elder, to the beloved Gaius, whom I love in truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Beloved, I pray that in every way you may do well and be in good health, just as your soul is doing well.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I was overjoyed when brothers and sisters came and testified to your truth, how you are walking in truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have no greater joy than this: to hear that my children are walking in the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Beloved, you act faithfully in whatever you do for the brothers and sisters, and strangers at that,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who have testified to your love before the assembly. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for they set out for the sake of the Name, taking nothing from the pagans.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We therefore ought to take such people in, so that we may become co-workers with the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I wrote something to the assembly, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first among them, does not receive us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason, if I come, I will bring up the things he is doing: talking malicious nonsense about us. And not content with that, he does not receive the brothers and sisters himself, and he stops those who want to and throws them out of the assembly.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Beloved, do not imitate evil but good. The one who does good is from God; the one who does evil has not seen God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Everyone has testified in favor of Demetrius, and so has the truth itself. We testify too, and you know that our testimony is true.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I had much to write to you, but I do not want to write to you with ink and pen.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I hope instead to see you soon, and we will talk face to face.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peace to you. The friends greet you. Greet the friends by name.

notes.note: The writer gives a title and no name, as in 2 John. The word can mean simply an older man, but it was also a recognised title for a community leader. Church tradition identifies the writer with the apostle John; many scholars leave the identification open.

A wish for the recipient's welfare and health was a standard opening in Greek letters of the period, and this verse follows that convention. It is a courteous greeting given a Christian turn by the comparison with Gaius's soul, not a general promise of prosperity. The older rendering 'above all things' for the opening phrase is now generally replaced by 'in every way' or 'in all respects'.

The Greek masculine plural was the ordinary way to refer to a mixed group, and here it means fellow believers. In this letter they are travelling workers, who may in fact all have been men, but the Greek does not say so. More formal translations keep 'brothers', often with a footnote that women may be included.

The Greek word was the everyday term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint's word for Israel assembled. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. The word here means the local community of believers meeting together.

The verb regularly meant more than saying goodbye. It covered equipping travellers for the next stage of their journey with food, money or companions. Gaius is being asked for practical support, which explains the remark in the next verse that these travellers take nothing from outsiders.

The Greek says simply 'the name', with no further identification. Most interpreters take it as the name of Jesus Christ, in whose service these travellers went out. The absolute expression echoes the Jewish use of 'the Name' as a reverent way of referring to God.

The word means people of the nations outside God's people. 'Gentiles' is the common rendering, but Gaius and his circle bear Greek names and were probably not Jewish themselves, so the contrast is with those outside the faith. Some modern translations accordingly use 'pagans' or 'unbelievers'.

The verb means to receive someone as a guest and so to support them. It is a compound of the verb for 'taking' in verse 7, and the play on words seems deliberate: they take nothing from outsiders, so believers should take them in. Most translations use 'support' or 'show hospitality to', which give the sense but lose the echo.

The Greek can mean working alongside the truth itself, treated almost as a person, or working alongside the travellers in the service of the truth. Many translations take the second sense ('fellow workers for the truth'). The first is chosen here because the grammar most naturally marks the partner one works with, and because verse 12 also speaks of the truth as an active witness.

notes.traditional: receiveth us not; does not acknowledge our authority
notes.note: The same verb is used in verse 10 for refusing hospitality to travelling believers, and the same English word is kept here. Applied to the elder, who is not present, it may mean that Diotrephes rejects his letter and emissaries or, as some translations put it, that he does not acknowledge the elder's authority. The Greek does not settle which.

Nothing else is known of this Demetrius. The threefold testimony reads like a formal commendation, and many scholars infer that he was one of the travelling workers and probably the bearer of this letter, whom Gaius is being asked to welcome. This is an inference, not something the letter states.

'Friends' as a name for fellow believers is rare in the New Testament, where 'brothers and sisters' is usual. It may echo Jesus calling his disciples friends in John 15. Some editions and translations, including the King James Version, count this verse as the end of verse 14, giving the letter fourteen verses.
